Variants.Content: The town of Keche is a coastal town in southern Westerlands. It is not a large port like Lannisport, but it has become a link in the maritime network of the West through small docks, fisheries, coastal shipping and surrounding estates. The fate of a port or town is often determined by invisible things: whether the sea currents are smooth, whether the price of salt is high, whether there are warships in the distance, whether grain ships can arrive in season. The people of Keche Town belong to the gold mines and vassal order of the West, as well as the tides and sailors' rumors of the Sunset Sea. It was a transit point for merchants, a home for fishermen, and a tax and coastal watch for lords.

Entry Kayce Local families also relied on mining tunnels, pastures, mountain roads, gold and silver circulation and the market sheltered by Casterly Rock; if any road, well or dock failed, the price would fall first on them.

Entry Kayce They also recognize the accents, laws, and credentials of the West; reputations can travel great distances from taverns, but true distances must still be measured by wheel, oar, or horse's hooves.

Entry Kayce If you can supply supplies, avoid danger, and find a guide, it is worth marking in your itinerary; if you don't have these three things, no matter how loud your family name is, it won't be able to save the lost.

The craftsmen saw ship repair wood, canvas, salt, fish catch and stones to resist the sea wind in the town of Keche. The priests guarded the stone carvings left by the Seven Gods, family tombs and the authority of the lords. A stronghold was therefore not just a lord's hall, but also a place where weddings and funerals, vows, labor and local memories recurred.

Entry Kayce They care about the mines, pastures, mountain roads, the circulation of gold and silver, and the market under the protection of Casterly Rock. They also look at whether seeds are left after the grain collection and whether the city gates are open in times of disaster. When people from afar see the coat of arms, what they see is whether there will be food to eat tomorrow.
